newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Young Russians loath to tie knot in changing times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Young Russians loath to tie knot in changing times.

text.p: Veronika and Maxim have long been in love, but wedding bells are just not ringing for the young Moscow couple.

"It's a must to live together before marriage to get to know each other," said Veronika Kayumova, 26, who has lived with boyfriend Maxim Pisarev for more than five years. "Also, we have friends whose relationships were ruined after they got married."

Russians, facing unprecedented freedom to live as they choose, are increasingly putting off marriage. Experts say they are either tying the knot later in life or choosing to live together without ceremony.
"Nowadays many men feel they should reach a certain status and achieve economic independence before getting married," said Tatyana Gorko, a sociologist at the Russian Academy of Sciences.
"Before, many couples got married earlier so they could legalise their sexual relationship."

Like many young Russians, Maxim is concentrating on building up his business as a middleman, arranging shipments of electronics to the regions. With the approval of Veronika's parents, he has moved into her room in the family apartment -- an arrangement far rarer for unmarried couples a generation ago.
"Before, society looked down on couples who lived together but now it is more relaxed about cohabitation," said Natalia Rimashevskaya, director of Institute for the Study of Socio-Economic Problems.
WE WANT MONEY, NOT MARRIAGE
Natasha Ketova, 21, followed her boyfriend Misha when he moved from Uzbekistan to Moscow a few months ago. But she draws the line at marriage.

"What if you had a big fight? You'd have to get divorced if married, but this way you could just leave," she said, adding that she had lived with Misha since she was 16. "For now we like things as they are."

In Soviet days, the state offered young couples like Natasha and Misha incentives to marry. While ordinary Russians searched bare stores, newlyweds received vouchers admitting them to special well-stocked shops.

Marriage also gave many couples a spot on a waiting list that eventually, perhaps years down the line, promised them their own apartment -- and a bit of privacy from parents and other relatives often living in overcrowded quarters.
The average couple who did not get married could not even rent a hotel room for the night, let alone dream of finding their own apartment.

In post-communist Russia, the desire to earn money makes the altar less of a lure to young people than in the past, resulting in half as many marriages in 1996 than in 1980, according to official statistics.

The average age of those getting married, including those making a return trip to the altar, is also on the rise. It is now 29 for men and 27 for women, two years older than in 1980, according to government data.
Although there are no statistics on couples living together, experts agree the number has risen sharply in recent years.

"Society is changing, and to a certain extent goals are changing," said Irina Zbarskaya, head demographer at the State Statistics Committee. "Before, young families were to a large extent tied to their parents, but now young people have more opportunity to earn money and be independent."
THE IMPACT OF RUSSIA'S SEXUAL REVOLUTION
Growing openness toward sex also makes the constraints of marriage less appealing for some Russians, experts say.

"There is a tendency toward more liberal sexual morals -- which was seen already in the 1970s -- and which has jumped markedly among teenagers," said Igor Kon, author of "The Sexual Revolution in Russia from the Age of the Tsars to Today".
Motherhood outside marriage is also on the rise, with 21 percent of all births in 1995 out of wedlock, compared to 11 percent in 1980, according to official statistics.
But some couples living together say having a baby would finally bring them together in marriage.

"If we had a child we would get married," said Maxim Pisarev. "Family values are not important if we just live together, but things would be different if we had a baby, otherwise he could grow up with complexes."

Kon, one of the country's foremost sexologists, added: "Today many do not have a legal relationship, and they only make it formal when they need to receive social benefits by registering the children."
AN OVERALL DEMOGRAPHIC CRISIS
The decline of the traditional marriage is part of what some politicians and experts are calling a demographic crisis, as fewer Russians are having babies.
The result is a shrinking population in this country of 150 million, and some fear Russia's population levels could dwindle for decades for come.
"To a certain extent the fall in the number of marriages does affect the birth rate, because a couple living together outside marriage is less oriented towards children," Zbarskaya said.
But other experts say recent trends are good for society, because marriage is becoming more considered and perhaps more lasting in a country where the divorce rate has long been high.
"The choice of marriage now is not romantic and traditional as in Soviet times but is more rational," said Gorko. "If people more conscientiously choose partners, of course it's better."
